newsitem.title: USA: U.S. backs peace process after N.Irish riot, arson.
newsitem.headline: U.S. backs peace process after N.Irish riot, arson.

text.p: The U.S. ambassador to Britain voiced support for Northern Ireland's struggling peace process after overnight rioting and an arson attack on a Catholic church on Wednesday.

In the latest in a string of sectarian attacks, vestments and the interior of a church at Annaclone, in County Down, were damaged by a deliberately-lit early morning fire, the fifth in two weeks at Catholic churches, police said.

The blaze followed overnight clashes between Protestants and Catholics near Lurgan, in County Armagh, where police fired plastic bullets to break up crowds throwing petrol bombs on a road separating rival housing areas.

Northern Ireland, destablised by guerrilla conflict over the future of British rule, has experienced months of rising tension during which rival gangs have struck at Protestant and Catholic churches, community buildings, and schools.

U.S. ambassador to Britain Admiral William Crowe, on a visit to Northern Ireland, expressed his government's backing for faltering multi-party peace talks and repudiated Irish Republican Army violence and church attacks.

"My president has made clear, in the strongest terms, that we will continue to work with the British and Irish governments, and the involved parties, to help promote progress in the multi-party talks," he said.
"We have repeatedly condemned the IRA's return to violence. We are equally appalled by recent attacks on places of worship."
Minor damage was caused on Tuesday to a hall used by members of the Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity, at Stewartstown in County Tyrone.
Last weekend eight Catholic families fled an apartment block in north Belfast after attacks by Protestant "Loyalists" who want Northern Ireland to stay British.
According to police, arsonists have damaged 53 churches, 47 community buildings and 71 schools over the past 17 months.
IRA guerrillas who ditched a 17-month truce last year are waging an escalating campaign to end rule from London and unite Northern Ireland with the Irish Republic.
A ceasefire by Protestant guerrillas is unstable and "Loyalists" have been blamed for two killings and a spate of random attacks on Catholics in the past year.
Security sources fear more sectarian flare-ups in the run up to a disputed series of traditional summer marches by hardline Protestants. "It's heating up," said one officer.
Multi-party talks aimed at finding a political settlement in Northern Ireland have been suspended until the British election on May 1 is over.
